_readme: Per-repo translation POLICY for the shared i18n guards, read by
check-locale-coverage.ts and by both ingestion scripts via --policy.
Committed rather than passed on the command line: restating a rule
per run is how it becomes a reflex, and a flag people always pass
guards nothing.
requiredLiterals — strings the app compares TYPED USER INPUT against.
A locale that translates one renders a gate no speaker of that
language can pass. Enforced at ingestion because surfaces at risk
include apps with no coverage guard of their own (apps/defi's
recovery page compares against the same word).
omissions / empty — the narrow linguistic exemptions, bound to the
exact locale:key(:token) so each excuses itself and nothing else.
acceptedAsTranslated — leaves whose value is CORRECT even though it
matches the English word for word, so the match is not evidence of a
gap. Each entry carries a written reason AND the English value it
was granted against: if en.json moves on, the exemption goes stale
and is reported rather than silently inherited. Most entries are
identical to the English; where a locale is instead built from the
same words in a different order (French 'Mode strict' for 'Strict
mode'), record that exact value under 'values' so rewording it
retires the exemption instead of leaving it armed.
The same scope also excuses a fragment that correctly holds no words
at all because a sister fragment carries them (see footerParts.tail).
There are deliberately NO pattern-based exemptions. Punctuation is
localized (consentParts.suffix is '.' in English and '。' in
Chinese), so a no-letters rule would have let a real localization
regress unnoticed. Everything else identical to English belongs in
english-valued-baseline.json, which is meant to shrink.

ar:copy.units.durationDay_two.reason: Arabic dual encodes the count in the noun (يومان = 'two days'); restating {{count}} renders '2 يومان'

ar:copy.units.durationMonth_two.reason: Arabic dual encodes the count in the noun

ar:copy.units.durationYear_two.reason: Arabic dual encodes the count in the noun

empty.ja:copy.consentParts.prefix: Japanese puts the verb last; the suffix carries the agreement the English states up front

copy.analytics.total.reason: "Total" is the ordinary Spanish and French noun for a sum, spelled as the English one. The evidence that each bundle was localized rather than skipped is the siblings around it — the same section renders "Activos"/"Actifs", "Reembolsados"/"Remboursés", "Liquidados"/"Liquidés" — so this leaf is settled vocabulary. Recorded here for the same reason as copy.notifications.title: a translation already correct can only leave a shrink-only baseline by being replaced with a worse synonym.

copy.app.name.reason: The product name. A brand is not translated.

copy.chrome.nav.positionsShort.reason: "Positions" is the correct French plural of "position" — an ordinary French word spelled as the English. The same-language sibling copy.chrome.nav.positions is "Mes positions", which uses the identical noun, so this is settled French rather than an untouched string. Recorded here for the same reason as the notification labels: it is a translation already done, and a shrink-only baseline could only lose it to a worse synonym.

copy.claimAll.itemLabel.reason: French numbers an item with 'n°' where English uses '#'. The English here has no words at all, so the marks are the whole content and a novel mark cannot be read as evidence of translation — this exact French is approved instead. The other eight locales still carry the English '#' and remain recorded in the shrinkable baseline, each owing its own convention (German 'Nr.', Spanish 'n.º').

copy.claims.row.amountWithSuffix.reason: Two interpolated values and nothing else — there are no words in this string.

copy.consentParts.suffix.reason: The closing fragment of the consent sentence, which is split into a prefix and a suffix. Arabic, German, Spanish, French and Korean all end a sentence with '.', so their correct localization is the same mark the English uses; Hindi, Japanese, Tamil and Chinese put the closing verb or clause in the suffix instead, and their exact endings are recorded below. In every case the sibling copy.consentParts.prefix is fully translated, which is the evidence that the sentence was localized and these endings are deliberate rather than untouched strings. All nine are named because the English here has no words at all: the marks are the whole content, so 'not the English marks' cannot be read as 'translated', and every value has to be one a person approved. Recorded here rather than in the shrink-only baseline because a translation already correct can only leave that list by being replaced with a wrong mark.

copy.desk.positions.tab.reason: "Positions" is the correct French plural of "position" — an ordinary French word spelled as the English. The same-language sibling copy.chrome.nav.positions is "Mes positions", which uses the identical noun, so this is settled French rather than an untouched string. Recorded here for the same reason as the notification labels: it is a translation already done, and a shrink-only baseline could only lose it to a worse synonym.

copy.desk.signed.rateLine.reason: Two interpolated values around APR, itself a standard finance acronym; there is no prose here to translate.

copy.desk.statUnknown.reason: The em dash marking an unavailable value on the trading desk (DeskHeader, OrderTicket). It is a symbol, not a word, and all nine locales render it identically on purpose — recorded here rather than in the baseline because it is not debt anyone can pay: the only way it could ever leave a shrink-only backlog is by being replaced with a different glyph, which would be a regression rather than a translation.

copy.desk.ticket.expiryGtc.reason: GTC — standard order-duration acronym, used untranslated on trading surfaces in every locale.

copy.desk.ticket.fillAon.reason: AON — standard fill-type acronym, used untranslated on trading surfaces in every locale.

copy.desk.ticket.fillIoc.reason: IOC — standard fill-type acronym, used untranslated on trading surfaces in every locale.

copy.diagnostics.title.reason: 'Support' is the ordinary German and French noun for this, spelled as the English one. The evidence is the sibling in each bundle: copy.diagnostics.open reads 'Support und Verbindungsprüfung' in German and 'Support et vérification de connexion' in French, so each locale uses the word inside a sentence it did translate — settled vocabulary, not an untouched string. Spanish is deliberately absent: it says 'Soporte', and Hindi stays in the shrinkable baseline because it owes a Devanagari rendering.

copy.notifications.bellLabel.reason: "Notifications" is the correct French plural of "notification" — an ordinary French word that happens to be spelled exactly as the English. Recorded here rather than in the shrink-only baseline because the baseline is a worklist of translations someone owes, and this one is already done: the only way it could leave the baseline is by being replaced with a less natural synonym, which would be a regression.

copy.notifications.title.reason: "Notifications" is the correct French plural of "notification" — an ordinary French word that happens to be spelled exactly as the English. Recorded here rather than in the shrink-only baseline because the baseline is a worklist of translations someone owes, and this one is already done: the only way it could leave the baseline is by being replaced with a less natural synonym, which would be a regression.

copy.offers.footerParts.tail.reason: The closing fragment of a sentence split around two inline links. English trails the sentence with the noun (' flows.'); German, Spanish and French put that noun in the LEAD fragment instead ('… wie die gefuehrten Ablaeufe ', '… los flujos guiados de ', '… les parcours guides '), so the tail is correctly nothing but the full stop. The words are present in the rendered sentence, just in a different fragment — which is what splitting a sentence into parts costs, and a per-fragment check cannot see.

copy.protocolConsole.bpsValue.reason: Two interpolated values, the percent sign, and "bps" — the standard basis-points abbreviation this codebase uses on every fee surface, and a glossary term that stays untranslated. There is no prose here to render in another language, so a value made of the same marks is the correct localization rather than an untouched string. It is NOT invariant: German, Spanish and French insert the space their typography requires before %, and Japanese and Chinese use fullwidth parentheses — real localizations of a string whose only content is punctuation, recorded below so changing one retires the exemption instead of leaving it armed. Arabic, Hindi, Korean and Tamil correctly keep the English marks.

copy.protocolConsole.hoursValue.reason: A duration built from placeholders and the SI unit symbols "h" and "s", which are the same marks in Spanish and French. The locale values are not byte-identical — both insert the non-breaking-style space their typography requires before a unit — but the guard compares words, and a symbol shared with the English cannot be told from an untranslated one. German is deliberately absent: it says "Std.". Recorded here rather than in the shrinkable baseline because "h" IS the Spanish and French rendering; the only way out of a worklist would be to replace a correct symbol with a wrong one.

copy.protocolConsole.minutesValue.reason: As hoursValue: placeholders plus the SI unit symbols "min" and "s". Spanish and French use the identical abbreviation; German capitalizes and abbreviates it as "Min.", which the word comparison folds back onto the English "min" — a real localization the guard cannot see. All three carry their own spacing, recorded below.

copy.protocolConsole.secondsValue.reason: One placeholder and the SI symbol for the second. There are no words in this string at all; the three locales differ from the English only in the space their typography puts before a unit symbol.

copy.riskAccess.strict.title.reason: French 'Mode strict' is the correct rendering of 'Strict mode' — the noun-adjective order is French grammar, and both words are French. The guard asks whether everything the reader sees is made only of the English source's own words, in any arrangement, so it cannot tell this from a rearranged English sentence; the accepted French is recorded below so rewording it retires this entry.
